title: Bloomington school

definition.text: A research tradition in political economy, built around Elinor and Vincent Ostrom at Indiana University Bloomington, that studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems.

facts.text: It focuses on governance, collective action and institutional diversity, especially for common-pool resources, decentralisation and self-governance.
The Ostroms founded its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, in 1973.
Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990) challenged the 'tragedy of the commons' by showing communities worldwide managing common-pool resources successfully.
Her research named eight design principles for successful commons, among them clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution.
Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it.
Critics say its findings are hard to scale up to national or global levels and that it underplays power and inequality.

contested_note: Some economists doubt Ostrom's commons findings scale up, and critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.

definition.text: Governance by many overlapping, independent decision-making centres operating at different scales, rather than by one central authority.

facts.text: Vincent Ostrom argued such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving.
It challenged the usual choice between central government control and privatisation, suggesting self-organising systems often beat top-down solutions.
Elinor Ostrom proposed that key management decisions be taken as close as possible to the events and actors involved.
Some question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.

definition.text: A process for managing coasts sustainably that works across geographic and political boundaries and weighs natural, social and economic systems together.

facts.text: The concept was developed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio and set out in Chapter 17 of Agenda 21.
Coastal margins cover 8% of the world's surface but provide 25% of global resources, and about 70% of people live within a day's walk of the coast.
It runs in five steps: situation assessment, plan, institutionalisation of the plan, implementation and ongoing evaluation, with no end state.
Its main constraints are institutional rather than technological, and treating the coast as common property hampers top-down control.

definition.text: The diplomacy, mechanisms and responses aimed at steering societies to prevent, mitigate or adapt to the risks of climate change.

facts.text: Modern international climate governance rests on three pillars: mitigation, adaptation and means of implementation.
A defining milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which sought to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement each country submits its own nationally determined contribution, which is not legally binding.
The North–South divide between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
It works across supranational, national, regional and local scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts as actors alongside states.
It increasingly relies on market mechanisms, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, clean development mechanism and joint implementation, alongside command-and-control rules.
A country that stays out of an agreement can still benefit from others' emission cuts without acting itself.

definition.text: The ways institutions evolve to meet a community's needs as its environment changes.

facts.text: Introduced by Holling in 1978, it is a flexible approach to climate impacts that contrasts with mitigation-focused efforts.
New institutions would strengthen the resilience of linked climate and social systems so they can adapt and stay stable.
It is mainly bottom-up, built on community-based action.
